title: Teen Invents Plant-Based Plastic That Eats Microplastics
summary: Microplastics are tiny bits of plastic that are almost everywhere — in oceans, soil, food, and even the air. They're so small that removing them is super hard. But 18-year-old Arya Satheesh from Ireland has a clever idea. She invented Eco Purge, a plant-based plastic that breaks down naturally while also helping break down microplastics already in the environment. Arya first got interested in microplastics in 2024, when she built a water-quality sensor for a science competition. Her device could find microplastics, but it couldn't remove them. So she decided to fix that. To make Eco Purge, she needed two natural enzymes. Some companies wanted to sell them, but they were too expensive for a high school student. So Arya emailed Professor Kevin O'Connor at BiOrbic in Ireland. He got her the enzymes and let her use a university lab. By early 2026, she had a prototype. She tested it in soil, salt water, and fresh water. After six weeks, both the microplastic and Eco Purge had decomposed. Her invention won the European regional title at The Earth Prize in May 2026, plus $12,500. Arya says: "Science isn't just about understanding the world. It's about leaving it better than we found it."
why_it_matters: Arya started with a school science project and ended up with a real invention, which shows that kids who spot a problem nearby — like plastic in a local river — can get help from adults and labs to do something about it.

background_read: Scientists have found microplastics in the ocean, in rain, and even inside human blood — they mostly come from plastic bags, bottles and clothes wearing down into tiny bits.
An enzyme is a natural molecule that speeds up a chemical reaction; your body uses enzymes to break down your food.
Ireland (a country in Europe, west of the United Kingdom) is where Arya lives, and BiOrbic is a science research centre there where scientists study materials that do not harm nature.
The Earth Prize is a competition that gives money and support to young people around the world who have ideas for helping the environment.

perspectives.description: They believe science should leave the world better than we found it, and that a cheap, natural material can clean up pollution that is very hard to remove.
Six weeks in a small test is only a first step, so some would want to see Eco Purge tested on real beaches and oceans before calling it a solution.
Companies that make ordinary plastic may worry about costs and change, but they could also see a new product to sell and less plastic waste to clean up.
